transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-18 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (CTO, Aurelius), Sara Wu (Infra), Mohan Iyer (Security), Lena Ortiz (SRE)

Summary (auto):
- Deep dive on Private VPC networking, control-plane connectivity (PrivateLink vs TGW), egress patterns (NAT gateway, egress-only), DNS/resolver options, and runtime implications (KV cache placement, batching, quantization).
- Identified next steps: share arch diagram, run perf microbenchmarks, schedule hands-on workshop, Aurelius to provide VPC details.

Topics: PrivateLink, NAT, subnets/route tables, resolver endpoints, KV cache AZ placement, batching strategy, quantization impact on latency

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we've got about an hour, we wanted to go deep on the private VPC setup and then tie it back to runtime stuff like KV cache and batching, we'll try to leave 10 minutes for q's at the end
[00:12] Tom: yeah appreciate it, we are trying to understand tradeoffs. our main questions are around: can we avoid public egress for model downloads and telemetry, how PrivateLink looks for control plane, and the latency impact if KV cache sits in a different AZ
[00:28] Priya: got it. quick agenda: 1) control-plane connectivity options (PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway), 2) egress and NAT choices, 3) DNS and resolver endpoints for model artifact fetches and runtime name resolution, 4) runtime considerations - KV cache placement, batching, quantization and kernel selection. sound right?
[00:45] Sara: yep, makes sense. also want to understand security posture: mTLS, KMS, audit logs - can we get those in the private deployment?
[00:52] Alex: absolutely, we'll cover the control-plane auth and KMS options; there is a security whitepaper we'll share.

[01:05] Priya: starting with control plane: for Private we offer two patterns. simplest: PrivateLink endpoint in your VPC that talks to our managed control plane through an interface endpoint. pros: no internet egress, fine-grained SG rules. cons: single endpoint per region and you need to connect route tables correctly. alternative is site-to-site or TGW peering for larger orgs that prefer central routing. TGW makes sense if you already have cross-account routing and many VPCs.
[01:36] Mohan: one question, does PrivateLink carry model artifact downloads or only API/control traffic? we want model artifacts to be pulled from S3 in our account, not Redwood
[01:44] Priya: good point. artifacts ideally live in your S3. our agent in your VPC pulls model blobs from your S3 using roles you create; control-plane API calls can go over PrivateLink. if you want zero public egress, you put a VPC endpoint (gateway) to S3 and block internet egress via route tables + NACLs. model pull latency then depends on S3 throughput and placement in AZs.
[02:05] Lena: so the agent lives in our VPC? what about the inference runtime, does that sit in our subnets too?
[02:12] Alex: in Private deployment both control-plane agents and model runtime (the serving nodes) are deployed into your VPC/subnets; we can run them in customer-managed subnets so you control SGs/NACLs. the runtime needs access to the GPU nodes; if you use our on-prem package it's similar.

[02:30] Tom: about AZs - if KV cache is in AZ-a and the request routes to a runtime in AZ-b, what's typical latency penalty and what's recommended?
[02:38] Priya: good question. KV cache is latency-sensitive because missing keys result in fetching large context from disk or re-computation. typical intra-region AZ RTT is 1-2ms on modern clouds, under ideal config. but e.g., cross-AZ egress through NAT or extra hops can add 5-10ms. for tight tail-latency SLOs (p99 < 250ms) we recommend co-locating KV cache and serving pods in the same AZ and prefer AZ-aware placement in the scheduler.
[03:06] Sara: ok co-location sounds right. what about replication? if we co-locate per-AZ KV and replicate asynchronously, what's the consistency/impact?
[03:14] Priya: we do async replication across AZs by default for availability; that keeps write latency low but you could see eventual consistency on a very small fraction of requests. for strong consistency we can route reads to the primary but that increases cross-AZ traffic and can spike tail latency. most customers choose AZ-local reads + async replicate to keep latency predictable.
[03:35] Mohan: can you quantify bandwidth and cost? we want to estimate cross-AZ charges and NAT gateway costs if we go through internet for artifacts
[03:43] Alex: yes. cross-AZ replication bandwidth is typically modest relative to tokens per second unless you have very high churn in KV entries. we'll provide a sizing matrix in the spreadsheet. NAT gateway costs for egress are per-GB; if you lock artifacts in your S3 with VPC endpoint you avoid SNAT to the internet. many customers use a combination: PrivateLink for control, S3 VPC gateway for artifacts, and then NAT gateway only for ops telemetry to specific destinations if necessary.

[04:12] Priya: moving to DNS - two patterns: use your resolver endpoint (AWS Route53 inbound/outbound resolver) or run a local caching resolver in the VPC. important to ensure SRV/hostname lookups to internal registry resolve fast. if you have split-horizon DNS, ensure the agent uses the VPC resolver and we recommend TTL settings low enough to handle failover but not so low that you add DNS QPS load.
[04:38] Sara: we run a private Route53 hosted zone and have outbound resolver endpoints - sounds like that works. any special SR-IOV or ENI considerations for high-throughput nodes?
[04:46] Priya: from the network side, increase ENI count and ensure jumbo frames if your infra supports it; again we'll detail those in the arch doc. for very high throughput you may prefer placement groups and enhanced networking.

[05:05] Alex: now linking networking choices to runtime: KV cache miss means you pull KV pages (which could be dozens of KB) and then run token generation. batching helps amortize lock/coord overhead across requests, but increases tail latency if you wait too long. quantization reduces per-token compute latency but can change memory access patterns and affect kernel selection.
[05:25] Priya: specific numbers from our benchmarks: on rtx/gpu-like hardware, 8-bit quant reduces per-token compute time by ~20-30% at the cost of slight quality degradation depending on model. KV cache colocated in same AZ reduces p50/p95 by ~3-7ms compared to cross-AZ. batching of small requests (batch size 4-8) gives best throughput/latency tradeoff for multi-tenant workloads; very large batching only benefits high-throughput low-latency-tolerance use cases.
[05:55] Tom: do you have an example of a producer-consumer config for batching? we want autoscaling to add capacity without huge cold-start penalties
[06:02] Priya: yes, we use continuous batching in the runtime: each worker keeps a short batching window (configurable 10-50ms), if the queue fills earlier it flushes. autoscaler pre-warms based on request rate signals and has a fast warm path using cached model artifacts and warmed KV pages. we can tune the eviction policy to keep hot prefixes in memory and minimize cold-starts.
[06:26] Sara: about private endpoints - route tables: do you prefer dedicated subnets per role (control-plane, runtime, mgmt) or shared? and SG recommendations?
[06:34] Alex: dedicated subnets per role is cleaner for auditing and least-privilege. e.g., control-plane iface endpoints in a management subnet, runtime in private subnets with no public route, and a bastion or transit subnet for ops. SGs: allow only necessary ports (TCP 443 for control-plane, gRPC ports between runtime nodes), zero-trust model: mutual TLS for all control-plane comms.
[06:57] Mohan: auditing - can we ship audit logs to our CloudTrail bucket?
[07:01] Priya: yes, logs can be configured to write to your logging bucket; we support KMS-managed encryption keys and can integrate with your SIEM via forwarders.

[07:15] Alex: quick demo-ish architecture note: shared slide link: https://redwood.example.com/private-vpc-arch.png (we'll share the actual deck). this diagram shows PrivateLink for control, S3 gateway endpoint for artifacts, per-AZ runtime + KV caches, and a service mesh for intra-cluster security.
[07:32] Tom: looks good. a couple of edge cases: 1) what if we have intermittent cross-AZ network flaps, 2) what about DNS poisoning if someone changes internal entries?
[07:41] Priya: for flaps we rely on exponential backoff + local hot-cache; we can also configure fallback to a healthy AZ but that increases latency. for DNS tampering, use VPC resolver auth and restrict who can update zones; also sign requests internally where possible.
[07:58] Sara: one more, on quantization: if we do 8-bit q we might see model output drift, how do you test regressions?
[08:06] Alex: we have an Optimize pipeline that runs eval sets on quantized variants and flags regressions. typical flow: baseline eval against your prompt set, then quantized model run; regressions above threshold trigger a rollback to float or alternative quant profile. we'll share the eval harness and sample reports.
[08:26] Mohan: about SLAs - if we want p99 latency SLOs, what deployment pattern do you recommend?
[08:33] Priya: p99 SLOs are best met with AZ-local placement, conservative batching windows, and redundant replicas per-AZ. Reserved capacity (Dedicated) gives stronger guarantees since you won't be contending with shared pool. we'll map SLA tiers to instance counts in the sizing spreadsheet.

[08:55] Alex: ok let's recap next steps and owners. Alex will share deck and whitepaper; Priya will run microbenchmarks and share perf spreadsheet; Aurelius to provide VPC CIDR and AZs; Mohan to confirm KMS/encryption policies. we'll schedule the workshop for hands-on network validation.
[09:13] Tom: thanks all — appreciate the level of detail. expect our infra folks to send the VPC details by Monday.
[09:20] Lena: quick note, we'll try to give sample prompts for evals as well so you can run the quantized regressions against our workload.
[09:26] Alex: perfect. thanks everyone.

[09:35] End of recording
